issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

vignette: John, a 55-year-old European-American male and a counselor, has been struggling with PTSD following a man-made disaster that occurred several months ago. The trauma he experienced has significantly impacted his daily life, making it difficult for him to maintain relationships and perform his job duties. The traumatic event unfolded during a workshop John was leading at a community center. A gas leak ignited in the basement, causing an explosion that filled the building with smoke and flames. John vividly remembers the acrid smell of burning material and the choking sensation as he tried to navigate through the thick smoke to evacuate his participants. The experience left him shaken and forever changed his perception of safety. Since the disaster, specific triggers have become potent reminders of the event for John. When he smells burnt materials or even the faint hint of smoke, it instantly transports him back to that terrifying moment. The sound of objects being thrown, which often accompanied the chaos during the evacuation, also provokes a strong reaction. These sensory cues trigger intense emotions and distressing memories. To cope with these triggers, John has developed several maladaptive strategies. He avoids seeing friends because he fears they might inadvertently bring up aspects of the disaster that could trigger his emotional responses. Moreover, he tries to avoid thinking about the event altogether, as he believes dwelling on it will overwhelm him emotionally. This constant monitoring and avoidance have become habitual, forming a cycle that exacerbates his distress. The memory of the traumatic event is fragmented and disorienting for John. When he thinks about the frightening incident, he can sometimes smell the burnt materials again, bringing back those visceral sensations. At other times, he feels the full emotional intensity without any clear visual imagery, making it feel as if the experience isn't his own but belongs to someone else. This alienation from his memories has further reinforced his negative appraisals. John’s body reacts as if he is still in danger even when he is safe, and this constant vigilance has taken a toll on him. He believes that being especially careful is necessary because you never know what could happen next. These beliefs have made it difficult for John to fully engage with the world around him. His fear of not being able to handle thoughts about the event leads him to avoid situations where he might be reminded of it. The interplay between these components has created a self-reinforcing cycle. When triggered by smells or sounds, John’s memories become more intense and distressing, leading him to feel even more vigilant and fearful. This heightened state makes his maladaptive strategies necessary, as they offer temporary relief from the overwhelming emotions. However, these strategies also prevent him from processing and integrating his traumatic experiences in a healthy way. John's work as a counselor has been particularly affected by this cycle. He finds it challenging to maintain focus during sessions, often preemptively steering conversations away from topics that might trigger reminders of the disaster. This has strained his relationships with colleagues and clients, making him feel increasingly isolated and ineffective in his role. What finally brought John to seek help was a realization that his coping mechanisms were no longer sustainable. He is most afraid of losing control and becoming unable to function at all. At the same time, he hopes for a way to regain a sense of stability and peace, allowing him to reconnect with others and resume his work without being constantly haunted by the memories of the disaster. In therapy, John aims to address these core issues, understanding that his fears are valid but also finding healthier ways to manage them. He is eager to explore how he can process his traumatic experience in a way that allows him to feel safe and present again in his daily life.
